title: Analyzing Organic Reactions
description: Use acid–base, donor–acceptor, kinetic, and redox reasoning to predict reactions.

sources.label: Supplied Kaplan curriculum: Chapter 4; section scope checked against local body and summary

review.note: Original explanations and exercises; source-backed author review, not independent expert verification.

lessons.label: Acid–base reasoning
lessons.title: Acid–base reasoning
lessons.tag: Equilibrium favors the weaker acid/base pair

cards.rule: Brønsted acids donate H+ and bases accept it. Lewis acids accept an electron pair; Lewis bases donate one. For HA + B ⇌ A− + BH+, K ≈ 10^[pKa(BH+) − pKa(HA)] when the pKa values use comparable conditions.
cards.cue: Lower pKa means stronger acid. Stabilize the conjugate base to increase acidity.
cards.trap: Basicity is an equilibrium property; nucleophilicity is a reaction-rate property. Do not use a single periodic trend across different solvents or unrelated functional groups.
cards.app: A carboxylic acid with pKa 4.8 is mostly carboxylate at pH 7.4; that changes water solubility and membrane partitioning.

steps.label: 1. Locate the acidic group
steps.text: Removing the carboxyl O–H proton gives a carboxylate whose negative charge is shared across two oxygens.

diagram.caption: Illustrative monoprotic acid speciation; adjust pH.

steps.label: 2. Compare conjugate bases
steps.text: An alcohol-derived alkoxide lacks the equivalent two-oxygen resonance of a carboxylate. This is a major reason simple carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols.

lessons.label: Nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups
lessons.title: Nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups
lessons.tag: Electron pairs move from donor to acceptor

cards.rule: A nucleophile supplies an electron pair to an electrophile. A leaving group takes the bonding pair when it departs. Stable weak bases usually make better leaving groups. Protonation can turn poor leaving group OH− into neutral water.
cards.cue: Find electron-rich donor → electron-poor acceptor → possible leaving group. Curved arrows start at electrons, not positive charges.
cards.trap: A carbonyl oxygen is electron rich while its carbon is electron poor. A positive charge is not required for electrophilicity. Polar protic solvents strongly solvate small anions; polar aprotic solvents often increase their SN2 reactivity.
cards.app: Enzyme active sites position nucleophiles and electrophiles while stabilizing charge; the same donor–acceptor logic applies.

steps.label: 1. Polarize the bond
steps.text: Bromine withdraws electron density from the attached carbon. The C bonded to Br is the electrophilic site for substitution.

challenge.prompt: Select the electrophilic carbon bonded to Br.
challenge.explanation: B is polarized toward partial positive charge by bromine.

steps.label: 2. Follow bond cleavage
steps.text: In substitution, a nucleophile forms a bond to the electrophilic carbon while the C–Br bond ultimately breaks with its electron pair going to Br. Conditions determine whether this is concerted or stepwise.

lessons.label: SN1 vs. SN2
lessons.title: SN1 vs. SN2
lessons.tag: Mechanism depends on substrate and conditions

cards.rule: SN2 is concerted backside attack: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile], with geometric inversion. Methyl and unhindered primary centers are favorable. SN1 ionizes to a carbocation: rate = k[substrate]; tertiary, allylic, and benzylic stabilization can help.
cards.cue: SN2: two species in the rate law, one concerted event. SN1: slow ionization, then attack.
cards.trap: SN1 can rearrange and often racemizes a stereocenter, but ion pairing can prevent exactly 50:50 products. SN2 inversion does not guarantee an R↔S label change if CIP priorities change. Strong bases and heat can make elimination compete.
cards.app: Use a rate change to distinguish mechanisms: doubling nucleophile concentration doubles an ideal SN2 rate but does not alter an ideal SN1 rate.

steps.label: 1. Inspect crowding
steps.text: The carbon bonded to Br is tertiary, making backside SN2 attack strongly hindered. In a suitable ionizing solvent, ionization can lead to a tertiary carbocation.

steps.label: 2. Compare a primary site
steps.text: A primary carbon is less crowded. With a strong nucleophile in a suitable polar aprotic solvent, bromoethane is a much better SN2 candidate. A primary unstabilized carbocation is unfavorable.

lessons.label: Organic oxidation and reduction
lessons.title: Organic oxidation and reduction
lessons.tag: Track bonds to H and electronegative atoms

cards.rule: Oxidation of carbon usually increases bonds to O/N/halogens or decreases C–H bonds. Reduction does the reverse. C–C bonds contribute zero when assigning carbon oxidation states. PCC under anhydrous conditions can oxidize a primary alcohol to an aldehyde; aqueous strong oxidants can give an acid.
cards.cue: More bonds to O, less H: carbon is oxidized. Hydride addition to C=O generally reduces it.
cards.trap: NaBH4 commonly reduces aldehydes and ketones but ordinarily not esters or carboxylic acids. LiAlH4 reduces a wider set, including esters and acids, with appropriate workup. Reagent conditions matter.
cards.app: NAD+/NADH couples biological alcohol/carbonyl oxidation states through hydride transfer; not every laboratory reagent has a direct biological analogue.

steps.label: 1. Alcohol carbon
steps.text: For the CH2OH carbon, one C–O bond contributes +1 and two C–H bonds contribute −2: oxidation state −1.

steps.label: 2. Aldehyde carbon
steps.text: For CHO, C=O contributes +2, C–H contributes −1, and C–C contributes 0: oxidation state +1. Alcohol → aldehyde is a two-electron oxidation.

steps.label: 3. Ketone reduction
steps.text: Hydride adds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon; protonation of oxygen gives a secondary alcohol.

lessons.label: Chemoselectivity and a reaction workflow
lessons.title: Chemoselectivity and a reaction workflow
lessons.tag: Choose by reactivity, not naming seniority

cards.rule: Inventory functional groups, identify reagent roles, locate the likely reactive site, account for solvent and acid–base steps, then track bonds and stereochemistry. Chemoselectivity means preferential reaction at one functional group.
cards.cue: Group inventory → reagent → first step → bond changes → product checks.
cards.trap: The group with the highest naming priority is not automatically the most reactive. Under ordinary NaBH4 conditions, a ketone can be reduced while an ester survives. Protecting groups change electronic reactivity, not merely steric bulk.
cards.app: Acetals protect aldehyde/ketone carbonyls from many basic and nucleophilic conditions; aqueous acid restores the carbonyl.

steps.label: 1. Inventory two carbonyls
steps.text: This molecule contains an ester at the left and a ketone at the right. The ester has an oxygen substituent directly on its carbonyl carbon.

steps.label: 2. Predict a selective step
steps.text: Ordinary NaBH4 conditions favor reduction of the ketone. Ester resonance donation lowers its electrophilicity relative to the ketone; a stronger reducing system can change the outcome.

challenge.prompt: Select the ketone carbonyl carbon targeted preferentially by ordinary NaBH4 conditions.
challenge.explanation: D is the ketone carbonyl carbon; A belongs to the ester.

exercises.label: Estimate acid–base equilibrium
exercises.title: Estimate acid–base equilibrium

stages.prompt: Select both oxygens of the carboxyl group.
stages.explanation: C and D are the two carboxyl oxygens.
hints: Locate C=O and O–H on the same carbon.
Select the two O labels.

stages.prompt: If pKa(HA)=5 and pKa(BH+)=10, equilibrium favors…
stages.explanation: The product acid is weaker; K ≈ 10^(10−5).
hints: Compare the two acids.
Equilibrium favors the side with the higher-pKa acid.

stages.prompt: Estimate K for those pKa values.
hints: Subtract reactant-acid pKa from product-acid pKa.
Raise ten to that difference.

exercises.summary: A five-unit pKa advantage favors products by about 10⁵.

stages.explanation: B is attached to electronegative Br.
hints: Look for the carbon bonded to the leaving group.
The polarized C–Br bond identifies it.

stages.prompt: Which species supplies a lone pair as a nucleophile?
stages.explanation: OH− can donate an oxygen lone pair.
hints: Nucleophiles are electron-pair donors.
A negative charge often indicates available electrons.

stages.prompt: When C–Br breaks heterolytically, the pair goes to…
stages.explanation: The departing bromide takes the bonding electron pair.
hints: A leaving group retains the bond electrons.
Bromide is a relatively stable anion.

exercises.label: Mechanism and kinetics
exercises.title: Mechanism and kinetics

stages.prompt: With a strong nucleophile in polar aprotic solvent, this primary halide favors…
stages.explanation: The accessible primary carbon favors backside attack.
hints: Assess steric access and carbocation stability.
An unstabilized primary carbocation is poor.

stages.prompt: If both substrate and nucleophile concentrations double, by what factor does the ideal SN2 rate change?
hints: Use rate = k[substrate][nucleophile].
Each concentration contributes one factor of two.

stages.prompt: At a chiral SN2 reaction center, the geometry undergoes…
stages.explanation: Backside attack gives geometric inversion. R/S labels require a fresh CIP ranking.
hints: The nucleophile approaches opposite the leaving group.
Think of an umbrella turning inside out.

exercises.summary: SN2 is bimolecular and stereospecific for geometric inversion.

stages.explanation: B is bonded twice to oxygen.
hints: Find the C=O bond.
Choose its carbon endpoint.

stages.prompt: What is this aldehyde carbon’s oxidation state?
stages.explanation: +2 from C=O and −1 from C–H gives +1.
hints: Assign electrons in C–O to O and in C–H to C.
C–C contributes zero.

stages.prompt: NaBH4 followed by protonation converts it to…
stages.explanation: Hydride reduction of ethanal gives ethanol.
hints: Hydride adds to C=O.
The oxygen remains in the alcohol product.

exercises.label: Select a reactive site
exercises.title: Select a reactive site

stages.explanation: A is bonded to both carbonyl O and single-bonded O.
hints: An ester has C(=O)–O–C.
Find the carbonyl with a second oxygen neighbor.

stages.prompt: Select the ketone carbonyl carbon preferred by ordinary NaBH4 conditions.
stages.explanation: D is the ketone carbonyl carbon.
hints: The ketone has carbon substituents on both sides.
The right-hand carbonyl is more readily reduced here.

stages.prompt: Why not simply select the highest-priority naming group?
options: Naming seniority does not determine kinetic reactivity
stages.explanation: Chemoselectivity depends on electronic effects, reagent, solvent, and conditions.
hints: Naming and reaction mechanisms solve different problems.
Compare resonance donation and electrophilicity.

exercises.summary: Ketone reduction can leave the ester intact.
